utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Everyone is here, seems to be here. Yes, same composition as yesterday. One minor, one a little bit more important, or more important. I just want a confirmation from you for the record, Mr. Josse, that the confidential motion you filed yesterday has been withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It has, Your Honour. Indeed, I was going to rise as a preliminary matter and do that formally. The court officer has been very helpful and advised me that I really needed to do it in this way. I'm grateful to Your Honour. It's withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Josse. So you will recall that last Thursday an issue was raised in regard to a number of photos; to wit, photos showing aerials and aerial installations and different localities. And I had decided at the time, in consultation with Judge Prost, who was here, that such like issues on the admissibility of certain documents ought not to be decided during the sitting itself, when one of the Permanent Judges is not present. We believe that admissibility of evidence goes to the heart of the rules of evidence, of the procedural requirements upon which the case would ultimately hinge so we took that decision. We are now going to address formally the matter as raised, plus other issues that have been raised or reiterated since then relating to documents that have not been included in the 65 ter list of the Prosecution, issues that have been reiterated even up till yesterday and we are going to rule on these issues. So, please, I'm going to take you back for a moment to first some -- one of the unresolved issues regarding the documents proposed for admission by the Prosecution in relation to Witness PW-130. That's the witness we had last week, end of last week. The Defence objections to those exhibits were originally raised in the absence of Judge Kwon, and as I have explained we have now had an opportunity to discuss matter fully and are in a position to decide on the matter. With reference to Exhibits P02298, P02299, P02300, P02301, P02302, P02303, P02304, P02306 and P02307, that is the photos that I have referred to some minutes ago, despite the absence of a 65 ter number, the Defence were given notice of the Prosecution's intention to use those photographs and they had the opportunity to fully cross-examine on them. All these documents, therefore, are being admitted. As is also evident from our decision yesterday, with reference to Exhibits P02315 and P02316, the handwritten notebooks which were subject to the same objection, while they will be marked for identification purposes only, this is on the basis of the general caveat relating to intercepts and not for the other reasons advanced by the Defence teams per Mr. Bourgon and Mr. Ostojic. The question of their admissibility will eventually be governed by our general ruling. The remainder of the intercepts for which objections have been raised on the basis of translation issues, we trust and we are fully confident that there are ongoing discussions between the Defence and Prosecution that hopefully can resolve all pending issues in this regard. Now we are handing down a -- what we consider to be an important ruling for your guidance. For future reference, while we are following the practice of dealing with objections to exhibits at the end of the witness testimony, if there are issues such as alleged lack of adequate notice or surprise, those issues should in fact be raised at the earliest opportunity, that is in advance as much as possible, as has indeed been done on several occasions but on some occasions this hasn't been the practice. In this way, the matter can be addressed before the document or whatever the document is, before the document is shown to the witness, and at a time when there are various alternatives available to address any problems that might arise. So please be guided by this rule in future. Normal admissibility issues will be covered at the end of the witness. However, if there are issues that are particular to a document in a way that should be addressed before, preferably before the document is shown to the witness, please come forward at the earliest opportunity so that we avoid unnecessary controversies and perhaps injustices later on. Okay. We left you yesterday with an exhortation and in the hope that there will be some kind of rapprochement meetings between the two sides with a view to resolving the issue of the exhibits that -- documents that the Prosecution wishes to tender, which ones need to be translated and which ones don't need to be translated and we will be going through that again. Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Counsel, ladies and gentlemen. We did undertake yesterday to identify those documents that required additional translation beyond the translation that had been provided, and we did identify very minor distinctions between the translations that -- of one document versus another, particularly in the areas where one translation was provided essentially for two documents. I have made certain corrections and modifications, I would say, to the tender list in toto which I have just discussed earlier with counsel for Mr. Nikolic, who had raised the objection yesterday. We have not resolved the issue entirely yet, and I don't want to waste any of the Court's time so my hope was to revise the list, send a copy of it to opposing counsel, discuss any issues that might be extant and then from that point simply come back at some later point when it's convenient for the Court and then offer the list of the documents to tender in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think that is a positive approach, Mr. Vanderpuye, which has the support of the Trial Chamber, and we'll give you all the opportunities and all the time you require to finalise this exercise in collaboration with the Defence teams, for which we are grateful. Any further preliminaries? I notice Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. In relation to that, Mr. President, and my upcoming witness, the Prosecution will endeavour to identify what I'm calling relevant changes from the notebook to the printout, and where we find those changes, we will provide additional translations and so we'll have -- each intercept will be either identified as no relevant changes or, if it does, it will have a translation that goes along with it, and I think that will hopefully clear up the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Mr. McCloskey. All right. I see Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I do have several objections with respect to Rule 65 ter number witness 76, which is the one after this witness, and I just want to let the Court know that, so whenever the Court would like to address that before he testifies, Mr. Thayer from the Office of the Prosecutor had sent me an e-mail last night about five to 10.00. I responded to his e-mail, and I set forth some of my objections to him. I wasn't sure if he was going to begin tomorrow or today, but I know there is one witness before this one, so I just wanted to advise the Court on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Today we are number 82.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Who is after him?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: 76, I believe, Your Honour. Only witness that remains.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so, yes. All right. How long do you expect this witness, 82, to be testifying?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I hope less than a half an hour on direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's you. But the Defence have indicated four hours in total.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He's similar to yesterday's witness so perhaps a similar thing will happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let me consult, please, with the other two Judges whether we should hear the submissions from Mr. Ostojic now or later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could get Mr. Thayer here to take part in that. I'm not sure if he's listening but that won't take long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you repeat, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. If you want -- if that issue is going to be dealt with I should get Mr. Thayer here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Now, we'll proceed with the first witness now, and after the break, at the beginning of the second session, get Mr. Thayer here, please, and in the meantime we would have had an assessment of how long the various cross-examinations are going to last, and we'll decide whether to hear your submissions then. But in that case, they will be at the beginning of the second session. All right?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So we have this next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome to this Tribunal and to this trial. You're a Prosecution witness. Madam Usher is going to hand you the text of a solemn declaration that you are required to make before you can give evidence before this Tribunal. It's a solemn declaration that you will be testifying the truth. Please proceed with reading out that solemn declaration and that will be your undertaking with this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Please make yourself comfortable. Take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, come as near the microphones as much as possible. Very briefly I'm going to explain to you what's going to happen. First of all, you will -- you have been granted some protective measures, namely the use of a pseudonym, that is you will be referred to by a number, you are Prosecution Witness 137, and also, we have decided to -- not to show your face to the outside world. So we have visual distortion or facial distortion in place. I think this has been explained to you. I just want to know whether this is to your satisfaction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. McCloskey will be the first one to ask you questions. He will also be referring to a statement that you made to the Office of the Prosecution sometime back, and then you will be cross-examined by the various Defence teams. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. If you could first take a look at what is marked P02326, that's the pseudonym sheet, and can you confirm that that is your name on that sheet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And can you confirm that within the last few days you were in my office and had a chance to review a signed statement you gave to the Prosecution back on 16 November 1999? Have you had a chance to review that statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And is that statement true and correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if you were asked to give that statement again, would the information in it basically be the same?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I am going to read a brief summary of that statement and for part of it we should go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we go into private session straight away, Mr. McCloskey? Because you didn't say which part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. If we could start off in private session, then I think I can get out after about a couple paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The witness worked at the northern site through the rest of the war and followed the orders and procedures of his command in receiving, scanning, taping and transcribing radio communications and all other aspects of his work at the northern site. These procedures included listening to an intercepted conversation, transcribing it into a notebook, which to do properly required replaying the tape recording of the conversation several times, and typing the conversation from the notebook into a computer and then encrypting it. Sometimes he would dictate his notes to the typist, thereby verifying its accuracy. If a portion of a conversation was inaudible, he would place dots in the notebook. In January 1996, he was demobilised and resumed civilian life in Bosnia. And if we could go into private session just for another couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: During 1995, can you tell us, did you obtain a particular certification as a ham radio operator?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes. Category B.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And in the last few days, have you had a -- were you provided a packet containing 15 intercepted conversations, including handwritten notebook entries and typed printout entries of those handwritten entries?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you able to compare and look at -- or excuse me, were you able to look at the handwritten entries of those 15 intercepts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Of those 15 intercepts, how many of the 15 did you actually recognise your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So is number 15 your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is there any doubt that numbers 1 through 14 were your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Without doubt, it's my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, just a couple of questions. We've -- and the Court has seen quite an a bit of these intercepts, but can you tell us what are the different ways that you can identify who is speaking in a particular intercept?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Most frequently, it went through the switchboard operators who were linking certain participants in the conversations. They would introduce themselves at the beginning of the conversation. That was based on that. And some of them, I recognised by their voice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you spoke -- briefly in your statement, but I just want to -- can you describe to the Court how you would generally, once you had transcribed a conversation into a notebook, what was the process whereby the notebook was put -- what was the next step after you transcribed the intercept and were finished? What was the next step as you took the notebook to the next step in the process?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: The next step was to take the transcribed intercept to the crypto protection service and then he would send the reports to the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how would you -- how would you do that with the crypto person normally? Would you just leave it with him? Would you participate in that? How did that work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: In most cases, I would read the intercepts to him myself. He would note them down and then he would apply the crypto protection, and then send that on to the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And so as you were reading it to this person, were you looking over anything that he was doing or were you just reading it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: I would be just following on the monitor, whether he made a mistake, compared to what I was reading to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now last night did you have a chance in my office to -- in working with an interpreter from our office, to have that interpreter read the printout version while you followed along and read your handwritten version?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And had I asked you to identify any mistakes that may have been made in the printout version that might have potentially changed the meaning of the -- some part of the intercept?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And in three different intercepts, we identified small mistakes; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to one intercept. It's intercept number 3 in the packet. It's from 16 July at 7.06 hours, and if we could -- I think we can put up the English and the B/C/S on the screen. That's 65 ter 1183. Okay. And the first thing I want to ask you about is that we -- I'm not sure if you can read that. Is it possible to make the -- just the top half of it bigger? We see when we look at this intercept that in the top of it, under participants, it says, Vinko Pandurevic/X, but that as we look at the text of the intercept, we don't see Mr. Pandurevic's name mentioned, his last name mentioned, that is. Do you know how it was that you were able to identify Vinko Pandurevic as a party to this conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: It's standard practice at the beginning of the conversation, they would generally introduce themselves, so then I was able to establish that it was Pandurevic. But here you cannot see that it's transcribed because in most cases I didn't note down that introductory part, but it's there on the actual recording.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me go to the B/C/S version, if you could look at the printout, and if you could go about ten lines down. And do you remember that a word that was in the notebook, it was missing in the printout at this -- at this point? Do you remember which one that was? And I can refresh your recollection, if -- I don't want you to have to go through the detailed comparison again, but we can if that's required. And I can tell you that on that line in the notebook, there is the word "gore" present. Do you remember reading the word "gore" in the notebook and identifying that it is not in the sentence on the printout?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And in this case, that would be referring "gore" --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, means something to the effect of "up there" in the English version. The term "up there" was left out of the section.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I'm going to have to object to Mr. McCloskey testifying. He's brought this witness here and let the witness testify. I strongly object to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm thinking you're perhaps right, but it's de minimis. But go ahead, Mr. McCloskey, please, and let's allow the witness to deal with these matters rather than you yourself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Actually I had difficulty which "gore" you meant. There are several "gore" in the handwritten note, and I see a "gore" in the printout as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I asked him to refer to the 10th line in the printout. It's my understanding that there -- on that sentence in the handwritten section, there is a "gore" but it is not in the printout.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Witness, if you could confirm that take a look at the printout --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 10th line from where?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I start at X, where it says "a ti si sefe." But we can have the witness confirm that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's basically the first line of the transcript proper, no? If I am reading you well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Witness, can you read the -- from your notebook the sentence that begins "imao sam" and just read it slowly and we'll see if we hear a word "gore" in that, and if we can try to follow along in our non-B/C/S heads, could you just read that slowly? In the notebook where you see it says "imao sam." It should be about line 10 as well.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: "I had self-propelled guns up there deep in the rear and now they took them." This is what is written in my notebook.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat. There was no microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we turn the witness's microphones on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher. All right. I think the microphones are on, from what I can see from here. We can proceed. But you need to repeat your answer, Witness, because the interpreters didn't catch the entirety. So the question was -- the interpreter said if he could repeat. What I have here is: "I had self-propelled guns up there in the rear and now they took them. This is what is written in my notebook." But then you said something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We can try it again and get all the puzzles in place now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you just again read slowly that sentence that you just read and we'll get a translation of it so we'll be clear.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: "I had these two self-propelled guns up there deep in the rear and now they took them."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now if we look over in the 10th line of the printout, we don't see the word "gore"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So that would change this conversation that Mr. Pandurevic was left -- that his self-propelled guns that were taken were not up there in the -- they were -- that -- the "up there" is mentioned in the handwritten version but not in the printout; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to another intercept, and if we could -- that is intercept number 5, which is a 17 July intercept at 12.00 noon, and if we could -- it's 65 ter 1215.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could have the printout and the notebook brought up. And for the Court and witnesses, the English line that I'll be asking about says, "I have regular communications is being established now with 2nd Battalions, I have radio."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So, Witness, if you could look at the -- well, we'll get to the 12 -- the conversation at the bottom of this page that begins at 1200 hours, if you could look at the -- both the handwritten version on the -- on the left, and the typed version on the right, I would point your attention to the second word in the second line. Can you slowly read us the second word as it is in the handwritten version?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: My written version, it says "has been established." In the typed version, it says "is being established." Meaning that it hasn't been established yet. But I have it as it has been established. So it's already -- it's in the past tense.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So we've got the same verb, we just have a tense different. What is the correct tense? Which one is correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: What is written is the correct version, the written version is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the last -- the last one that we've identified. And that is in conversation number 12, which is 65 ter number 1291, at 21 July, at 1030 hours, and if we could get the handwritten as well as the printout version, and we are going to go to the last four or five lines of this conversation. And, Witness, I'd ask you to look at the last -- as we get it up there on the screen, the last few lines, and for the English, I'll read the English translation of the area that I'm concerned with. It says: "And now they have come here and they say that yesterday they were to go and that there are -- that Risto Avdo is supposedly, hold the line and I'll report. Please stay on the line." Now, could you take a look at what's been marked in yellow. On the printout, we see Risto, which we have heard before in this Court is a first -- is a typical Bosnian first name, and we see in your handwritten word, the word "pristo Avdo." So could you read that sentence in your handwritten book using what you had written down just so that we can understand the -- what you heard and what you wrote down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: "And now they got here, they said that they were cut off yesterday from going, that there are, that Avdo has agreed it seems to negotiations."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So the word "pristo" means to have agreed and that's of course different from the first name of Risto.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Aside -- all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Yes, the Popovic Defence team, per Ms. Condon, will go first. Can I have more or less a revised assessment.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will definitely be finished within half an hour with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And the Beara Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Perhaps 15 minutes, Your Honour, no more than one half hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Nikolic Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Up to half an hour at the most, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Borovcanin Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 15 to 20 minutes, our estimate is, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Miletic Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About 15 minutes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Gvero Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Almost certainly nothing, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the Pandurevic Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear what the counsel said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No questions, so no need for interpretation. All right. Do you have the next witness here?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer and the witness are ready to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So we can start with the cross-examination by Ms. Condon, of course, and it's almost 100 per cent sure now that soon after the break, Mr. Ostojic, we will hear your submissions on the next witness. All right? Ms. Condon.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Your Honour, may we go into private session just briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session for a short while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Tell me, Witness, you also referred to having had equipment shortages while you were working at the unit that you were at. What sort of equipment shortages did you experience?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Could you please rephrase your question? It's not quite ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I'll remind you of something again that you said in your statement. What you said was: "It was possible for up to five operators to listen to conversations at once, but given equipment shortages it was more common for there to be two or three." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: In the beginning, yes, but later we received additional equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: And then four and even five operators could work at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, when you talk about four or five operators working at the same time, do you mean four or five operators listening, all listening to conversations at the same time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: I said that they could do that, but mostly two or three of them worked at the same time because the equipment was on scan mode all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, I want to ask you about that. In the shifts that you were working in, how many people were working in your shifts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Mostly in twos, sometimes it would be three, depending on the frequency of the conversations. If there was more work, then extra people would come.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, in relation to those two and three, what specifically all two or three of you were all scanning for the conversations at the same time, what were -- what roles were each of the two and three of you performing specifically?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: We would put the equipment on scan mode. If conversations started up, it would stop automatically. We would start recording on the UHER and then sometimes there would be nothing so we wouldn't be recording. That was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. In July 1995 at the unit you were at, how many tape recorders did you have that were functioning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly, but each set had at least four or five UHER machines, at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you say at this time you had four or five reel-to-reel tapes that were actually functioning; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. What about the state of that equipment? Was it in good repair? Did it break down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, no, it didn't break down. UHERs were second-hand; but as for other equipment, it was of a later date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, just in relation to the roles that each of you would play, what you've said is that normally you would have two or three hours of listening to a conversation and then you would break.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is that because obviously in the process of listening to the conversations, you're concentrating as much as possible; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then what would your procedure be? I'm not asking you about any of the other two operators. After you'd listened to two or three hours, would you then spend time transcribing the conversations into the notebooks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And while you were listening to the actual tapes, the conversations that you considered to be important you wrote down some information on pieces of paper; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. There has been evidence from other operators that while they were actually listening to the conversations, they would use pieces of paper to note down the frequency of the particular conversation, the time of the conversation, and the participants. Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in July of 1995, you were using the pieces of paper as well, were you, before you used the notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So once you -- you spend two or three hours listening and then you spend time listening again, writing down the conversations into your notebook; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Tell me, how many hours would that process take in relation to, say, for one conversation, that you want to get as accurate as possible, how many hours would that take to get that conversation down into your notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: It depends on how long the intercept was. I can't tell you now exactly. But it didn't take long to transcribe it, because one could hear the participants very well, so we didn't have to replay it five to six times. And if that was the case, if it wasn't clearly audible, then, yes, we would have to replay it and then the process was slower.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. But there has been evidence here that it would take up to 20 times to listen to a conversation before the transcription was correct. Would you agree with that, that sometimes it would take up to 20 times? You agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Even for relatively short, say, five- or ten-minute conversation, that process could take up to an hour and a half? You agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So and not only that, your particular practice, it seems, was to then -- once the conversation was written in your notebook, you would then dictate what was in your notebook to the typist; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Once my shift was over, I would take all the intercepts and my notebook and read it one after one, unless there was something interesting, in which case I would react immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, when you say "react immediately," does that mean that you would physically hand over the notebook to the typist and they could type it from your notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Tell me, was this process that you engaged in outside your shift of dictating your notebook to the typist, was that something that other operators at the unit did as well or was that something you just did yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Some people may have. Some maybe not. I really wouldn't be able to tell you. I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So it's fair to say that each of you had individual ways of transcribing what was in the notebooks to the typists, is that fair? Different ways of doing it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: No. There was one way to do it. We would take it. And when I had time I would go to the typist in order to help him, you know, to read it to him and so on. Otherwise, the procedure was the same: When the shift was over you would take the notebook to the encryptor and that was it. If I had time I would stay on to help them. People were not able to do as they pleased.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you would dictate what was in your notebook to the typist, would the two of you -- would the typist have their own input in relation to the conversation? Did that ever happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: The encryptor wrote down what I read out to him. [French coming over the English channel].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we need to -- I thank you, Ms. Condon, and I appreciate your patience, but we've heard all this in French, having the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Having the head phones next to our ears wouldn't allow us to be able to hear what's going on in English, too, so we need to have everything repeated, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'll ask you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you need to repeat your question and the witness will then --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Perhaps what I'll -- just so that I can clarify this with you, Witness, you would say that it was outside the normal procedure for you to dictate from what was in your notebook to your typist; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: That's not how I would describe it. I simply helped the encryptor in order to have the job completed as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In relation to the notebooks themselves, now, there has been evidence that the pieces of paper that the operators used were burnt. Is that -- you -- does that accord with your experience, that the pieces of paper that were used to note down the frequency, the participants and the time of the conversations were then burnt?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: I don't remember, and I can't give you an answer to that. I simply don't remember what happened to those papers. I threw them in the bin after copying the information into the notebook, and I truly don't remember any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. But I mean, there was obviously no order or instruction given from your command to keep those pieces of paper. That's clear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'll just go straight to the notebooks. In relation to the notebooks, what particular orders or instructions did you receive in relation to keeping the notebooks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: To write in the date, time, frequency, participants and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That wasn't my question, Witness. The question is this: In relation to the notebooks, what particular orders or instructions did you receive about keeping the notebooks, maintaining the notebooks at your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: The commander was always with us there. He would take the notebooks and place them in a designated location. I don't know where it was, but I'm sure that he knows about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We'll get to him. In relation to the use of your notebooks in your shift, how many -- between the two or three operators that were working at the same time, how many notebooks would be used amongst the two or three of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Everybody had one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Just so we make this clear, you all -- you weren't sharing one notebook? Each individual operator had their own notebook; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. There were two actually, but everybody would write in their own notebook. We knew the date, we would write down the frequency and this would be taken to encryptors and then they would forward it on. But generally, yes, we did have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, Witness, that answer is a little unclear to me. In the scenario where you have three operators at the same time, do I understand it that there were two notebooks that were in operation, not that you all individually had your own notebook. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Well, this is how it was. Let me clarify. There was one notebook for conversations which were current, that I was taking down. And, for example, my colleague, in order not to wait for me to complete my work, had his own notebook where he could record his own conversations without having to wait for me to complete my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. But when you say "his own notebook," this is one of the notebooks that you've been shown in your proofing session with Mr. McCloskey, the books that were used at the unit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So there is a situation that would happen where you would have two notebooks that were operating at the same time, being used at the same time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes. That could be the case, but one notebook was used most frequently, and the other one was used as needed. However, it was there on the desk.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned before in relation to the order, or the fact that your commander would take care of the notebooks, did the notebooks have to be filled before they would be handed over to your commander? As in completed, finished with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you've indicated that you weren't aware, within the unit, where the notebooks were kept; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I know that the commander would take them. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you aware whether or not any of those notebooks were ever burnt in the same way that the pieces of paper may have been disposed of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: That shouldn't be the case but I really can't answer because I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to ask you about a comment that you made in your proofing in 1999, whereby you indicated that -- or first of all I should establish this: Now it was the case that at the unit that you were at, there was a Ministry of Interior secret service unit operating as well, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you refer to them in that proofing note as the AID, and what you said was they were involved in the same kind of work as you were and on occasions he, being you, he would only be able to hear one part of a conversation but by comparison with AID, they were occasionally able to complete the loop. Now, do you recall telling that to one of the investigators, to the ICTY, in 1999?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is that correct? That's what used to happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Very seldom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, but the fact is you would share information with that service in relation to clarifying conversations that you might not understand; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Well, I will clarify. As far as I can remember, it happened perhaps just once, and I have very poor recollection of that. If I didn't hear the other participant well, then I would ask them whether they heard that voice clearly but I think that that happened only once. I don't really remember but that was all. I had no insight into their work, into what they were intercepting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I'm not asking you about what the target of their work was, just on these occasions that you would complete the loop, that was the expression you used, was it the case that they would come in and have an input into the conversations that you transcribed? Is that what would happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: I have very little memory of that, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Did your commander, was he aware of this -- just say it happened on one occasion, was your commander aware of the fact that the secret service were assisting you in this regard or did he not know about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Most likely he did, but I really don't remember this well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, what about the tapes that you used? What you indicated is that tapes were not in short supply in 1995. You recall making that statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But you also indicated that the decision was made at your unit to reuse some of the tapes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So it wasn't the case that all tapes were sent on to the command. That's not -- wasn't your experience, as you understood it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: All tapes were sent. They would take all the tapes. And I guess they did something, they erased something, and then we would receive the tapes again. That's all I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Perhaps can I remind you, because, Witness, that's not, in my submission to you, consistent with what you've said in your statement. What you said at page 3 was: "Tapes were in short supply and were reused unless the commander felt the conversation was so important it had to be sent to the corps command." Now, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes. That's how it was in the beginning, initially. The tapes were in short supply. But later on we had enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, in relation to the tapes themselves, can you give any evidence about whether or not the tapes were numbered in any way? Marked? Some sort of identification?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, I want to show you, please --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown on e-court, Your Honour, this is behind tab 7, and this appears at 1220. Could we bring up, if it's possible, 1220B and 1220E at the same time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to confirm that but I will soon tell you. Yes, it can be done. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, that's B on the right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Condon, I hate to be abrupt the way I'm going to be but something has cropped up that requires us to go downstairs to discuss something very urgent. If you could stop for the time being and then we continue immediately after the break. So after the break, of course, Ms. Condon will finish her cross-examination, and then we can do the -- in the absence of this witness, obviously. All right. We'll hear your submissions first, then you continue with your -- thank you. Half an hour, yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Once more my apologies, or our apologies to you, Ms. Condon, but we had an urgent matter relating to something completely different that we needed to attend to with some urgency before, certainly before 11.00. Mr. Ostojic, I understand from what you said earlier that you wish to address the Trial Chamber in relation to the next witness, that's witness number 76, who will be Prosecution Witness 133.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. Your Honour, the submission has multiple parts to it. Initially the first request we want to point out is that we are getting the summaries late and we are not getting them as agreed in a timely manner. As I mentioned previously, we received them late last night for the first time. This witness also doesn't have prior witness statements, and we are still hoping to get the NIOD statements from the Prosecutor when the time is appropriate. However, my objection goes to the heart of two issues. First of all, it's the impermissible use of purported intercepts that were transcribed by third parties, not by this very witness. The OTP, based on their summary, and it's my submission, is proceeding to seek to utilise in contravention of the Court's rulings both oral and written, as well as to circumvent the rules of procedure by doing so, the Court's ruling with respect to the evidence which addresses the acts and conduct of the accused should not be unilaterally ignored by the OTP or by anyone in this Tribunal. This clearly, in our submission, prejudices the fundamental rights and guarantees offered to the accused in this Tribunal. The Defence would be prevented from challenging and cross-examining these other purported intercept operators which are being unfairly used simply for two reasons. One to bolster the credibility of this witness, and to impermissibly substantiate his current testimony. At issue with this witness are three intercepts: One involves my client; the other two -- or all three involve General Krstic. OTP in their summary claim that there are other intercepts that this witness purportedly went in a different site in a different notebook, and they claim that now this witness confirms that he supposedly had overheard this conversation and the contents. They speculatively and impermissibly conclude that in fact based on their summary, that it was the same conversation. On its face it's not. I don't need to debate it with the witness. And what they are trying to do, Your Honour, is to come through the back door, if you will, and have us then challenge that testimony and bring in that evidence, which is not, number 1, our burden of proof or our duty to do. So we are asking this Court to restrict the Prosecutor from using this type of tactic when they know the rules are clear, if they want the intercept operator from the other sites to come in and testify in order to substantiate any theory they may have, then they should in accordance with this Court's ruling, in accordance with the rules, bring that intercept operator forward so that we can have the opportunity to cross-examine that witness as we were given with PW-133. That's our first submission. Secondly, Your Honour, we have an objection to the use of the Blagojevic transcript in this case. In the summary, clearly the Prosecutor is using the summary of Blagojevic as a further tactic to -- against the Defence and specifically my client. The three intercepts at issue involve General Krstic. It would be probably prudent, I would suggest, with all due respect that the Krstic transcript be utilised and not the Blagojevic transcript. The Blagojevic Defence team in my view rightfully did not challenge and the evidence adduced by this witness in the Blagojevic trial was unchallenged, rightfully so. The issue, they were not in the transcript, they were not in the intercept so they did ask several and a few questions. Interestingly enough, the Krstic transcript goes into detail on two separate occasions, both in 2000 as well as 2001 involving these intercepts. In fact, in the Krstic case, the Honourable Judge Riad and the Honourable Judge Wald both questioned this witness on critical matters, which the other Judges or Defence counsel or Prosecutor did not in the Blagojevic thing; namely the dating of the intercept. So I think if we want to have a fair process, if we want to protect the rights of the accused, the Krstic summary should be utilised and the Krstic transcript should be utilised as opposed to the Blagojevic transcript. This is a tactic by the Prosecutor to pick and choose their evidence and they then expect the Defence to during cross-examination to highlight or to explain away all these issues and points. It's impermissible to do that, I suggest to the Court. It's not the guidance -- or there's no rules to suggest that that's the manner in which they should proceed. Third, Your Honour, I would like to revisit the issue of a pseudonym for this witness and other witnesses. Although from time to time we did acknowledge and stipulate that the Prosecutor should in their discretion set forth if they believe that the witness should not have -- should not be revealed his identity, then he should be placed with a pseudonym. However, two things come to mind when we discussed this, and we raised it, I think, a couple weeks ago. One, the witness does not work in an area currently which would necessitate him to have any type of privileged or protected measures. It's clear from his background, which we won't have to go to into detail, what is the basis that this witness thinks that he deserves or is entitled to having a pseudonym? I don't find it there. It's important for us because other witnesses may come forth with evidence against this witness to go and attack his either credibility or his veracity as he may testify. Finally, Your Honour, I submit that the Prosecutor in some of their summaries have been quite inaccurate and have left it to -- the burden -- shifted the burden, actually, to the Defence to highlight or to try to explain those very inaccuracies. For example, in this summary there were several inaccuracies in the statement that the Prosecutor drew, yet they didn't make the comparison to the other transcript; namely, the Krstic transcript. This practice, I think, is putting an unfair burden on the Defence, and I think that is should be, with all due respect, stopped. But I'd like to just highlight for the Court that my first two submissions are the most critical. If the Court -- and if we had stipulated to the pseudonym, we understand that it could even constitute a waiver. We don't necessarily have a large objection to that, but I would like to emphasise that the third party intercept operators should not be allowed to be discussed with this witness as the Court has, in my view, restricted us from using other intercepts with witnesses, specifically the one where -- I think it was Exhibit 40, IPC, I think, 40, 41 and 42, and the second submission clearly with respect to the use of the Blagojevic transcript and the use of the Krstic transcript in its stead. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ostojic. Mr. Thayer? Let's take them one by one. The first point raised by Mr. Ostojic relates to the -- what he suggests is an untimely handing of the summaries. That's the first point. Not only as it relates to this next witness but also to the recent ones, as I understand it. Let's deal with that first.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. Good afternoon to you and Your Honours. Yes, things are moving a little faster than we had thought they might. I had a summary prepared yesterday morning. I wanted to wait until I was able to proof the witness in the afternoon, have him actually read this or have the summary read to him in a language that he understood. I notified counsel of that yesterday morning and then furnished the summary after I made a couple of corrections last night. Unfortunately, that's the hour it was done, necessitated by our proofing schedule. With respect to any inaccuracies in the summaries --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, let's take them one by one because there is more to it than that. It's also being suggested by Mr. Ostojic that, hope springs eternal, they are expecting from you the NIOD statements of this next witness. Have you made them available, when do you expect to make them available? Or have these been disclosed already?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No. We are in a very complicated process with NIOD trying to simplify it. This witness, as far as I'm aware, was not interviewed by NIOD, so that is not an issue with respect to him. The -- what we are trying to simplify with NIOD is a process in which they want to have contact with all the witnesses themselves, have the witnesses execute waivers, have the waivers sent back to NIOD, then have the statement released back to the witness so that they can make the decision about whether or not to release, as it were, this -- what's being considered Rule 70 material. I've been working very hard trying to shorten that procedure. They are not being particularly responsive. That's also been complicated with some absences over at NIOD. We are working on it; myself and an investigator on our team are working on it. We have had one person on our team personally contact every DutchBat officer for which we believe there was a NIOD statement, as well as the intercept operators that have testified to let them know that this procedure is under way, to cooperate as quickly as -- and as efficiently as possible so that we can move this along. That is the status of that endeavour, Your Honour. We are doing our best, but NIOD - and I must say rightfully so - seeks to protect the way it perceives was a confidential relationship that it had with some of its witnesses and at the very least wants to make sure that its witnesses or that the people that it interviewed understand what's going to happen possibly with the statements that they are furnishing to the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As I understand it, you feel almost 100 per cent sure that this witness did not give any statements to NIOD?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes. And I can reconfirm that, Your Honour. After this session, I can just run out, but that is my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does any of the Defence team have conflicting information on this? Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I don't believe so, Your Honour, but there is the first time we've heard that they were not. As we have seen with some other witnesses, that they have given testimony, both open and under a pseudonym with NIOD.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then there is the question of the proposed use of intercepts made by or carried out and transcribed by third parties. I think that's the first major issue raised by Mr. Ostojic. Perhaps you can address that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. I think as everyone can see from the exhibit list that we have furnished in anticipation of Witness 76's testimony, the list is radically simplified and reduced in size compared to what had initially been offered back or suggested back in October. That is precisely because I do not intend to offer through this witness intercept testimony that comes from other locations. We will be calling those witnesses in their own right. They will testify concerning those particular intercepts. So with respect to this issue, frankly, Your Honour, in terms of what I intend to lead the witness on, that issue has been mooted. Now, certainly, he was questioned about those intercepts in the Blagojevic case. That is where the intercepts came to light after they came to light some of them in the rebuttal case in Krstic. One of the reasons we decided to use Blagojevic is it's the most current testimony; that seemed common-sensical to us. It is one transcript as opposed to two, which would have been the case had we sought to use the Krstic testimony. The -- again, the evidence through this witness will be limited to the three intercepts which are contained in his packet, two of which I intend to discuss with him, and one which I do not intend to lead affirmative evidence upon. So all in all, Your Honour, I think that issue is frankly mooted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think in relation to this Blagojevic as opposed to Krstic previous testimony, I think there are other matters that you need to address. The suggestion on -- by Mr. Ostojic is that it's the testimony in Krstic and the testimony in Blagojevic and Jokic present two rather separate scenarios. His first proposition or objection is that it should, preference should have been made to refer to the Krstic testimony rather than the Blagojevic one. That more or less you have answered already. But what is your position in relation to the possibility of having both testimonies introduced? Because if I understand Mr. Ostojic well, he seems to be suggesting that in one case, certain issues were discussed during the testimony of this witness which were not discussed in another testimony, and if I read him well, although his suggestion is to prepare one rather than the other, if I read his submission well, if you want a complete picture of this gentleman's previous testimony on the whole gamut of areas he testified upon, you should have the two previous transcripts and not just one, or one rather than the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think practically speaking, while there may have been some areas that were gone into more so in Krstic and frankly more so in Blagojevic than in Krstic on others, I think the Blagojevic testimony most fairly encompasses the scope of this witness's testimony and fairly encompasses the vast majority of the Krstic testimony as well. I think frankly it would be confusing and burdensome to try to meld two entirely different trial transcripts into sort of one master summary versus just sticking with one transcript, and if Mr. Ostojic feels that there are areas that were not included to the degree he would have liked in the summary, then he's free to cross-examine. That said, Your Honour, I also intend to lead with this witness a couple of limited areas which were gone into detail more in Krstic than in Blagojevic. So to that extent I do intend to possibly cure some of that objection, but I frankly disagree that that is a compelling enough reason to try to mold together two separate trial transcripts when we have one that I think fairly captures what this witness's testimony was and will be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic can tender the Krstic transcript, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. In addition, because this is a very valid point that is being raised by my colleague Judge Kwon. In addition to that, there is also the submission that the way you have proceeded, and please don't misunderstand me, I do not in any way wish to contest the right of the Prosecutor to choose the evidence that it wishes to bring forward, but there is the suggestion, which I think is quite a valid one, that in doing so, in choosing Blagojevic only, and we have only heard now that you will also be addressing some parts of the Krstic testimony, you are increasing the load that the Defence teams have to carry, they being aware of the contents or the entire contents of this gentleman's testimony in Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- in Blagojevic, just to stick to the actual facts as they came out in Blagojevic, there was substantial cross-examination, first of all, on I would say the vast majority of the issues that were raised in Krstic. I don't think that there is any burden that's being shifted to the Defence unfairly in that case. We --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So your position is that in addition, this is not a dirty tactic that you sort of have adopted but --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may say so, the -- for example, my learned colleague raised an issue of the dating of the intercept not being discussed in Blagojevic and that's just not the case. The dating of the intercept was gone into in the Blagojevic case, and I think that when we see the testimony, when we see ultimately the cross-examination, and my direct, we'll be comfortable that the Blagojevic transcript fairly encompasses this witness's testimony. We are happy to introduce the Krstic transcript on its own in total, but it seems to me that respectfully that that would vitiate the time saving endeavour that we were hoping to have engaged in in creating a two-page summary for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. The issue of the pseudonym, what was the position in Blagojevic? Did he have protective measures in place?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, in both Krstic and Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that's all we needed to hear on that. And finally, there was a point made by Mr. Ostojic in relation to inaccuracies that, again, you are unduly burdening the Defence teams with identifying these when they could be included or pointed out in the summaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Frankly, Your Honour, I was trying to follow some of the examples that were laid out by my learned colleague, and I don't know whether he's reading a different summary, but I could not find what he purported to refer to in my summary. We stand ready as we always do. If there are perceived inaccuracies, those can be resolved ahead of time, and they can certainly be resolved during the testimony. I will read it. I will ask the witness to confirm whether there are any inaccuracies in it and he can be confronted with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We think it can be dealt with rather briefly, starting with the protective measures issue. I think we are governed first and foremost by the rule that we have that the protective measures already put in place in another case are carried forward, and when we decided to give him the two protective measures that you have there, we were doing nothing else but implementing the previous decisions, there being no new circumstances pointed to us which would make it important to refer to and decide upon. In relation to the first point, we would appreciate if you do your utmost, Mr. McCloskey, the whole Prosecution team, to make sure that the summaries are not only adequate but that they are also made available to the Defence teams in a timely fashion. We do acknowledge, as I hinted out when I first addressed you, that you have the right, which we will not interfere with, not even in this case, in this instance, to choose the way you wish to proceed and the evidence you wish to bring forward in relation to each witness, provided that is according to the law. You have dealt with the question of the possible use of transcripts made by others in a satisfactory manner, giving us also assurance that any transcripts made use, to be made use of now and hereinafter, you will bring over the person who made those transcripts, making him or her available for possible -- all possible cross-examination. The question about the Krstic transcript, we cannot of course impose it on you, because if you feel that the testimony of this -- the previous testimony of this person is thoroughly and satisfactorily covered in the Blagojevic trial and you wish to rely on that, then obviously we have to leave it at that, and then it will be up to the Defence teams in addition to what you may question the witness in relation to his other testimony, to cross-examine him on that. We of course leave all doors open. If it will become necessary to have the transcript of this individual in the Krstic trial introduced in the records of this case, we leave that option open. I think we have covered -- I think we have covered everything. I think we have covered everything. I think what is material anyway of substance. Yes. So that be it. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need to indicate as soon as possible about our possible remarks or objections in relation to the exhibits that are being submitted by the other side. So to that aim, I would like to say that Mr. Popovic's Defence would like to object to the exhibit that is on the list of the Prosecution for the examination-in-chief of the next witness, and that is exhibit marked as 1387G, and that's the 65 ter number. That exhibit is an audio exhibit. It has a number that has been assigned to it, but it's not indicated whether this is a tape, a CD, or a DVD. The second thing -- or the second reason why we object, and I would like to state this in advance in order to avoid any kind of misunderstanding that we believe that the -- this is not an authentic copy of the original. So as not to repeat my objection, that objection will apply to all the audio taped intercepts that the Prosecution are going to submit. I would also like to say that we don't know who made these copies, when they were made, and on which media they were made. This is the essence of our objection, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. I just would like to have a clarification from the Prosecution on this point. In relation to a previous audio that we heard in this courtroom, I think last week, there was an indication made by, either by you, Mr. Thayer, or by Mr. McCloskey, that the originals, quote/unquote, are in the vault, and that you are prepared to make them available as and when required. That is also applicable to this audio?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's absolutely correct, Mr. President. In fact, my understanding is that this audio to which my learned colleague refers is on the same reel-to-reel tape to which Mr. Nicholls referred last week with respect to his witness who had the audio tape. We stand ready to make that available if anybody who wants to hear it. It just requires an actual reel-to-reel tape to play. The medium on which it has been disclosed to Defence counsel and which we intend to play here is ultimately a CD which has been piped through our e-court system, and that's the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And will you be adducing evidence, testimony, in relation to these audios?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It was not my intention with this witness to establish any type of chain of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If -- I'm not necessarily referring to this next witness. I'm just referring to evidence which will go to prove to the chain of custody of this audio recording from stage one to wherever they have arrived now.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I think the bulk of that testimony has come in through Captain -- the previous -- one of the previous witnesses. With respect to this particular item, I don't think we've shown how it fits in to that witness's specific testimony, but this would be one of the items that he discussed during his testimony about - it's PW-131, by the way, for the record - how these pieces of evidence came into OTP's custody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I think we've heard enough. Ultimately this will be a matter that will need to be addressed and decided upon after we have heard all the evidence relating to the possible authenticity problems attached to such audio or audios, and I think if there are no further submissions, we can -- but I wish to thank you, Mr. Zivanovic, for having adhered to what we stated in the beginning of this sitting, to come forward in a timely fashion when you are objecting in a particular manner to some document that the Prosecution seeks to tender. Yes. Do you need to bring down the curtains while the witness is coming in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, we are going to continue. Ms. Condon will proceed with her cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I just want to establish that the protocol in relation to the notebooks was that you would write down the participants, the frequency, and the time of the conversation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when I use the word "protocol," you understand that that was as a result of specific orders that you received from your commander as to how you were to note down the conversations in your notebook; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, if you take a look at the document that's on the right, you have two documents in front of you, on the screen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: You mean my transcript or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No. On your -- the monitor that's on your right, there should be two documents in front of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, could you make sure that what he has --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see one document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, perhaps -- is there a document there that you recognise your handwriting? Does that make it easier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, at the top of that document, you'll see that there is a -- this -- there is a notation, channel 3; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And there are 12 -- it looks like 1249 H; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And there is no notation there as to the frequency of this alleged conversation, is there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes. But as written in the previous conversation, definitely. When the frequency is the same, then all you indicate in the next conversation is the number of the channel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want you to focus your attention on the line that appears ten lines down from the bottom, where it says, X, and then do you see that sentence there beginning, "I" and my pronunciation will be terrible. Do you see that, "i odma," those words there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, I want you just to read out, please, that sentence, from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: "And to have Goran go right away."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we just got the translation there. So Goran, tell me about that. That's a male name, is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: No. It says here "goram," not Goran, with an N.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. But what does "goram" mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: The words "goram" means "gore," which is up there. That's a typical localism for that area. Instead of saying "gore," up there, they say "goram."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So, in particular, and then this -- what you say is that it means go up there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: It says here: "To go goram." That's what that man uttered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, and then we'll see this is more for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, Your Honour, that in the document that is in English, at 1220A, the interpretation of that same line is: "And have him come here or/come/here/immediately."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, in relation to the question of voice recognition, Witness, can I ask you, did you ever have any formal training in voice identification?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No? So, in particular, you were asked in the course of this investigation by -- in -- I can -- in November of 1999, you were asked whether or not you were able to recognise the voices of VRS officers. Do you recall being asked that question?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
