utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how did that come about? Was particular officers's names suggested to you or did you volunteer them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Nobody suggested anything to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So in response to that question about whether or not you recognised voices of VRS officers, you said you were able to recognise several names, one of which was Popovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, it's obvious, isn't it, that unless a person identifies themselves in a conversation, you are relying on what you say is recognition of that person's voice. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Only if I was not sure would I put X or Y. If I was hundred per cent sure, then no. They mostly introduced themselves, but sometimes we would recognise their voices at the time because we heard them often.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But that actually wasn't my question. The scenario where a person identifies themselves, it's obvious that you can with 100 per cent certainty identify the participant. You agree with that proposition?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But in the scenario where a person doesn't identify themselves you're relying upon what you say is recognition of that voice over a period of time. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You also agree, don't you, that you did not personally know any of these people that you say you recognised their voice? You agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you also agree, don't you, that while you indicated that you could recognise the voice of Zivanovic, there was at least one occasion where you described his voice as being unintelligible? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Not that it was unintelligible. It was overmodulated and barely intelligible in one conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. You say "barely intelligible." I say -- I'm not going to get into an argument with you about that. What I'm suggesting to you, Witness, is that the process of you saying you recognise a voice is guess work on your part. Do you agree with that proposition?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: I wouldn't fully agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You would agree that without a person identifying themselves in a conversation, you can't be 100 per cent sure who the participant in that conversation is, can you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, in particular, you say that you recall conversations where one of the participants was Popovic. I want to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. I don't see that in any of his conversations.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: I accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: I'll rephrase.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That when you were asked the question about the voices that you recognised, you said that you were able to recognise the voice of Popovic. What about in July of 1995, Witness? Were there particular conversations that you say you recall whereby he was a participant?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Don't remember. Right now I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Were you -- let me ask you this: In the course of this investigation, were you shown notebooks from July 1995, that you had used?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in the course of being shown those notebooks, you did not see any notebooks that you had -- sorry, any conversations that you had transcribed whereby you could identify a Popovic as having been a party to any of the conversations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Could you reformulate that, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What you've said is that you have a specific recollection of recognising the voice of Popovic. You accept that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes, that year, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. And what I'm asking you about, in July of 1995, when you were shown the notebooks that you used, you did not see any conversations that you had intercepted during that period, where Popovic was a party, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Pardon me a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: I have no further questions of this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Condon. Is the Beara team going next? Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. How are you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Good morning. Thank you for inquiring. How are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I'm fine. I'd like to follow up on my colleague's question about specific recollections of intercepts. Now, you spoke with an investigator from the Office of the Prosecutor in 1999 by the name of Alistair Graham. Do you remember that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And didn't you tell him then specifically in May of 1999, four years after the events which transpired in July of 1995, that you did not recall any particular conversations of note?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, you were telling him the truth then, were you not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Naturally, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You testified earlier today that you had instructions in relation to the notebooks and that you were to write in the date, time, frequency, participants, of the conversations that you intercepted; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And did you follow that protocol and write the date each time that you listened to a conversation that was intercepted, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: The date would normally be recorded in the morning when the first conversation was recorded, and later on we would report -- record frequency and channel, so there was no need to enter the day every time. We would just do it with the first conversation and then we would know that everything else was done on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You just a moment ago testified when my colleague asked you whether or not you were suggested by the investigators for the Office of the Prosecutor any particular persons in regards to recognising their voices, you I think testified no, nobody suggested anything to you. Was that your testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So can I take it, then, that when you came in to give a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on 16 November 1999, that you just sat down and started talking?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, that's argumentative.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I beg to differ, Your Honour. It's not argumentative. If nothing was suggested to him, I want to know if he just started talking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's either flippant or argumentative. It's not the kind of question that's designed for an honest answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's a storm in a tea cup. Let's move on to the next question, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. I'd like to put several questions to you about the topic that you covered with Ms. Condon; namely, the identification of participants in the conversation. You testified today, and you explained to the Court and to us that you identified the participants when they introduced themselves, and when they did not introduce themselves then you weren't 100 per cent sure who they were. Would you please explain to me, in cases where you did not recognise the voices, and in cases where the participants did not introduce themselves, how did you identify the participants? How did you mark them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: In all cases where I wasn't sure about the identity of the participants, I would mark them with an X or a Y.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown tab 2, please? P2 -- 2327 A and 2327 B. Those are two versions, English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that you can see the B/C/S version on the right-hand side. This is one of the intercepts that you transcribed. Under the frequency indicated, 784, you marked the participants, Basevic Nidzo; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In the further text of this intercept, please look at it slowly, we see that none of the participants introduced themselves.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: In this particular case, they introduced themselves at the beginning of the conversation, which I did not transcribe. Or the switchboard operator, when making the connection, identified the participants, but I did not transcribe that initial portion of the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown tab 12, document 1291, C and B. Rather, C and D. I apologise, C and D because B is not a complete document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the problem?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1291 D needs to be on the ELMO. They cannot both go in e-court at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Partly on e-court, partly on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps it would be good if we saw the English version in e-court so that those who follow in English can see the document. I don't have it on my screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have it now? Do you have it now?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, I don't have it. I just have e-court, the English version, but for some reason I don't have what I need in order to discuss this with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher what we have on the screen, on e-court, at the moment is the English translation, starting 259.675 megahertz, 10.30 hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's the right document, and the witness should have the B/C/S version on the ELMO in front of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's being placed on the ELMO now. Let's see the heading -- yeah, okay. No. This is not the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we scroll down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That is when it starts. It's the last part, the last third part of the page that we are interested in.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Sir, would you be so kind and please look over these intercepts, which were recorded by you. They start with the names Lelek, Colonel Djurcic. This conversation goes on, on to the second page. Once again, none of the participants introduced themselves, nor did you indicate that you recognised the voices. Wasn't it logical for you to mark them with an X or a Y?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: No. No, it wasn't, because these conversations went through the switchboard operator, and the names of these people were given before I started transcribing it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: So you did not transcribe this portion of the conversation either?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Would you please look at the conversation on the same document that precedes it, beginning with 255850, Mitar Jevdjo. Once again, this is an intercept transcribed by you; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: I don't know because I don't have the version in my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In order to cover this as speedily as possible, I have that handwritten version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Can you for the time being also put on the ELMO superimposed on the other, the handwritten version, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is Exhibit 1291A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You need to put it further down, yes. No, no, that's too much. Yes. Stop there, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: This intercept, we already commented on, so could we scroll up a little bit so that the witness can see whether this brief intercept that was recorded -- so that he can see if that's his handwriting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes, it's my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The participants didn't introduce themselves either?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: So you didn't listen to this -- you didn't transcribe this entire intercept?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: So there are exceptionally many intercepts that you did not transcribe yourself, but you put the participants more or less approximately according to their names?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: No, it wasn't approximate. They would introduce themselves at the start of the conversation, that part was not important to me, and what you see is what I transcribed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Why was this part important to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: I don't have an answer for you on that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Nikolic. Who is next? Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like us to stick to the time and we are going to go through the documents. And we also need to speak slowly, I'm afraid, otherwise we will overlap, and we are talking about many nuances here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please now show the witness on e-court the intercept from tab 1? This is the 65 ter number 1161, A and C.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And while we are waiting, this is an intercept in which you participated, Zivanovic and Jokic. I would like to put a couple of questions to you about that. If I can just ask for 1161C to be shown at the same time or it can go on the ELMO. This is your handwriting; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At the end of this intercept, you put in a remark that you mentioned earlier today, General Zivanovic talked quite in an overmodulated way and quite incomprehensibly. Do you remember saying that? Can we scroll down a little bit, please, so that we can look at the bottom of this page? Can you now look at the last sentence, please? Is that your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It says there: "General Zivanovic spoke overmodulatedly and quite unintelligibly." Can you please tell us what does that mean, overmodulatedly and incomprehensibly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: The remark probably was prompted by the reason that the telephone used by General Zivanovic -- he was either speaking very loudly into the telephone, I don't know what was the matter with the telephone, but it was quite recognisable that he was speaking at that moment. Overmodulated could mean that he was speaking too loudly, that the phone was faulty in some way, so it was too loud, and quite unintelligibly meant probably that in that part it was difficult to understand what he was saying. Usually the conversations were quite well articulated. In such cases, I would call one or two of my colleagues to help. We would play it back a few more times, to make sure about what was actually being said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have notes about the characteristics of certain speakers that would crop up in the intercepts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: No. We didn't. Actually, I myself did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware if any of your colleagues had a file with voice or speech characteristics, accent, specificities, words that they would use, of certain participants in the intercepts that you were listening into?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you now look at the first line of this text that you jotted down, the one that you're seeing on the ELMO, where it states: "Z: I cannot get through." We have now moved it but -- all right. Very well. I think it's all right now. It's in the middle of this text, somewhere in the middle, it says: "Z: And then I cannot get through." Then there is a word inserted: "Gore, up there." "There are some of them up there," and so on and so forth. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Except it says here: "Is there anybody there, up there."

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: My question is: Do you see this word that is added, "up there"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you put that word in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And do you see dots underneath that word?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Am I correct if I say that while you were listening or transcribing, as the term here is used, you were not able to hear the word well, so you put those dots there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. Because I assume that the dots were there in the beginning but then later -- I mean, it was most often the case that if some word was not quite clear, two or three of us would listen, we would play it back a few times, all of us listening, and then that's how it came about that I actually put that word in.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So you will agree that you couldn't hear the word right away and that you put the dots there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: I heard the word, but I wasn't quite sure what the word was until we played it back several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And then you inserted the word?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that sometimes, when listening back to the intercepts, somebody else who heard the word better would add to the original text a word that he managed to decipher?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: No, no. That wasn't possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You were the only one who could have done that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you to look at tab 6, and if possible, maybe we can look at 65 ter number 1219A on the e-court, and 1219B. And while we are waiting, I just wanted to ask you something. When you came across nicknames, how would you note them down using capital letters or lower case letters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Well, it should have been put in in capitals.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If somebody's nickname is Bor, how would you write that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Like Bor, with the first letter B. The first letter would be capital, capital B.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If we can now look at 65 ter, both English and B/C/S versions. Do you see this in front of you now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is this your text?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please read this second sentence, actually, the second line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: You mean participant X?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: "Tell me, is Pop there?"

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And the answer is, if you can read it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: "No."

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In our language, is the word "pop" something that can mean priest as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Are we talking about a priest here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: I cannot give you an answer. I don't know what the participant wanted to ask. I wrote it down but I don't know what he was asking. I can't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So when you hear someone say, "Tell me, is Pop anywhere around," you are telling us here today that you cannot know whether he was looking for some priest or somebody whose name was Pop; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Well, I assume so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is priest, in our language, written with a capital letter or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: No, it's written out in lower case letters.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot really see that well. Did you use a capital letter here or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: I used a capital letter here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And to finish with this intercept, you marked that one of the participants was X and the other participant was Trbic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would it also be correct here that you identified this speaker, or participant, in the part of the conversation that you did not transcribe?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like us to look at tab 9. And if we can see on e-court 65 ter document 1238A and 1238B. And while we are waiting for these intercepts, I just wanted to ask you something. How often -- and now I'm speaking about you -- how often was it the case that you did not transcribe that section of the intercept where the persons identified themselves? Was that a rule of your work or an exception?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't a rule, but I considered that to be an unimportant part. I believe that it was important for them to introduce themselves and for me to note it down. Had I known that that would be a -- at issue here, then I would have noted that down as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But you would agree with me that your instruction was to literally record what you heard; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In such cases, as far as I understand you, you did not do that, but you skipped the part of the conversation where someone introduced themselves or was introduced by the intermediary centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Could you please rephrase that for me?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I will. In these cases, you did not act in accordance with the instructions, but you skipped over noting down the part of the conversation in which the speakers introduced themselves or were introduced by someone else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And were you told to do this or did you do this for practical reasons so that you would write less?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: We did it because that part was not interesting to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think this issue has been laboured and belaboured. I think we've heard enough on this, Mr. Stojanovic. I suggest you move to something different.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I am going to be finishing soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to look at this intercept. Can we look at the bottom section where it says that the participants in the conversation are Strbac, and then it says, Colonel Cerovic, and then -- that Cerovic is in parentheses with a question mark. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Should I clarify why the question mark is there?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is precisely what I wanted to ask you. When you read this part of the intercept, you have one participant who is introduced?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And so why is there a name here in parentheses with a question mark?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Because it's not 100 per cent certain, but while replaying the word seemed to resemble this particular word the most. That's why there is a question mark there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Which part of the conversation that you were listening to most resembles that word Cerovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Just like in the previous intercepts, it's at the beginning of the conversation. We possibly didn't transcribe it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. Stojanovic. Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you were talking about recognising voices. Would you -- or were you, rather, able to -- can you tell us how many times did you have to hear a voice before you were able to recognise a person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Several times, naturally. I don't know the exact number of times.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it right to say that it depends of the person, that for some people you were able to recognise their voices but for other people you had to listen to their voices many times in order to recognise them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, you talked about various intercepted conversations with the Prosecutor before you came to this courtroom, and you've identified three mistakes. Those mistakes that you identified, was it the Prosecutor who showed you those mistakes or did you identify them yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: I myself identified them.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did you examine carefully all the conversations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown Exhibit 1161B, please? And in English, it is 1161A. I would like the second part of the page to be shown, the lower part of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, can you see the sentence that begins with, "Ili da odu na Djurisice," to go to Djurisice?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you read this sentence, Djurisice,, is that a name of a village or is that a name of a person? Could you explain this to us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Probably -- I wouldn't know what to answer. It's hard. Probably it's a place.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown Exhibit 1161C? It's on page -- it's the document that ends with the page 808. It's the following page.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, do you see the sentence in which we can read, "Or they should go to Djurisice."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it exact to say that this sentence is not the exact same sentence that we just saw in the typed version?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In the typed version, the sentence talks, rather, of a place, and here we have the feeling that it is referring to a person; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown Exhibit 2327C? The English version is 2327A.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, do you see the name that is written down in the conversation that belongs at 619. The name is Bacevic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: This is a name that is normally written with two Cs, and both Cs have an accent; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown Exhibit 2327B?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, the same name is written down here with two Ss, but in Serbo-Croatian it would be an S with an accent on top; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can we then conclude that both names, the name that appears in the handwritten version and in the typed version, that those two names are not identical?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Actually, it is the same, but it's just a typographical error.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I understand, sir. I believe that it is a typo. But if we talk about those two names, it's two different names. One name is Bacevic and the other name would be Basevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's already told you that it's the same person, Madam Fauveau. He seemed to acknowledge also that it's a typographical error.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, but to change a letter in a name can designate another person, and this can bring to confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think there is room for any confusion at this point because the witness has already confirmed to you that it is the same person. I think we need to have a break now. We'll have a 30-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't repeat the same question. Move to something different, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us what is the real name of the person that you wrote down as being Bacevic? Is it Bacevic or Basevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown Exhibit 1214B, please? The second intercepted conversation took place at 11.15. That's the one that I would like to see on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, are you able to find the sentence that states that a person talked to a certain Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown Exhibit 1214D? It's the second page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, in the second line of this document, we can see that there is a person who is talking to another person called Kovac; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So there is a mistake here as well with regard to the name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Most likely the mistake is in the printed portion, not in the handwritten portion.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you were transcribing conversations in your notebook, were they written down in a chronological order?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: In most cases, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And when you say "in most cases," were there cases where the chronological order was not respected?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Sometimes some intercepts were transcribed in the other notebook. Sometimes that would happen. But in most cases, they followed a chronological order.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When a conversation was transcribed in a notebook, let's say it says 2200 hours and the next one is 8.00 a.m., does that mean that the 8.00 a.m. conversation was written down the day after the conversation of the 2200 hours one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When two conversations follow, if one takes place at 2200 hours, 10.00 p.m., and another one at 8.00 a.m., does that mean that the conversation that was transcribed at 8.00 a.m. was actually heard the day after, following the conversation that took place at 10.00 p.m. the day before?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If there is an actual notebook that this is a reference to, I think that would be appropriate as opposed to just a hypothetical which wouldn't be real relevant unless it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Correct. I think that would also make it easy for the witness who is giving me the impression that he is not exactly clear in his mind as to what you are asking.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Mr. President. Could the witness be shown Exhibit P2330, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, on this first page, is it right to say that we see 16th of July, 1995? I presume that this is the month of July 1995.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Most likely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Does that mean that the first conversation transcribed in this notebook took place on the 16th of July, 1995? Could we please show page 4 of this notebook. Sir, this is a conversation that is written in this notebook, the first conversation that was actually transcribed. Can we conclude that it was transcribed on the 16th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: From the notebook itself, I don't think he can tell you the date unless the date is indicated, which I -- I'm not seeing any date indicated there, at least from what I have on the monitor. So he would need to see the typed transcript in order to be able to tell you whether the date is the correct one or not. How is he going to tell you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, but there is a date on the first page of this notebook, so I just assume that he can tell us if this conversation could have taken place before the 16th of July or on a date following the 16th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is -- yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If he's allowed to look at the entire document, I don't think at this point, you know, making guessing games or at least provide a foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He answered he doesn't know. Let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm not sure I heard that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, he said he cannot. He said that. And I pointed out that of course he cannot. The date is not indicated against this transcript. He can't -- it will be sheer guessing or he must be a genius.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would be more than happy to show the notebook to the witness, because there is one particular conversation that appears in the document, which is typewritten on the 21st of July, and then there are ten dates that fall -- that took place before. So as of the first page of the document, one could conclude that the first conversation could not have happened between the 16th of July, so there is a big discrepancy between this document and the typewritten document. I cannot demonstrate what I mean otherwise than just to show the witness this notebook.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we shouldn't have any further discussions. Let's show the witness the notebook and then refer him to any specific parts from that notebook and put the questions that you need in order to possibly establish the date of this particular transcript that we see on the screen and any further questions that may become relevant or important. So who, Madam Usher -- the notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sure we can find it, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But that's not something we have a physical copy of right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. If I understood Madam Fauveau well, she is interested first in the cover. So let's see the cover and proceed accordingly. Then do you know the page -- okay. So yes. Can we see the next page, please? And the next. Yes. And the next. Yes, go on, please. Is there a way in which we don't have to go --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would be good if we could stop at page 6, please. A conversation took place at 2300 hours [as interpreted], 53, so 10.53 p.m., and on the following page, another intercept took place at 1148, so I assume even though we don't know the date of the first conversation, that this conversation took place the day after the previous conversation. And then I would like to go to page 9, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it just your assumption or are you putting a question to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm asking the question to answer -- I'm asking the witness to answer my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Would you agree, sir, that the transcript that you see on top of this page with a time of 11.48 goes back to a time later than the previous transcript that you saw on page 6, which had a time of 22 or 23.50 something? I didn't hear his answer. I think his microphones are switched off, at least one is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, we do have the book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Then perhaps we can hand him the book and Madam Fauveau can refer him to the various pages that she has in mind and we can then ask him the questions. And as you go along, we'll try to have the pages on the screen as well for us to be able to follow.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown -- or, rather, would you like me to start from the beginning or to start with the page that we were at?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would go straight to what you are trying to get the witness to confirm. So I think you said initially the whole purpose of this exercise was to try and establish that the first transcript that you showed him preceded a certain date.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In part, that's what I would like to establish. But the second part that I would like to establish is the following: Is that the conversation that appears on the document typed on the 21st of July, if you follow the logic that the witness described, according to which they were following a chronological order, then it would be the previous day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which page are you referring to? This transcript of the 21st of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness also said that it was not perfect, that they would sometimes write "other" in, so I don't know where this takes us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But let's not testify for him because he said that already and leave it at that. If Madam Fauveau is contesting that there is some indication in this notebook -- please tell your client to keep quiet because we will need to take certain measures otherwise. Yes, Madam Fauveau. Which page do you wish to refer this witness to in relation to the intercept of the 21st of July?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The page I would like to refer the witness to is 00801510, and there is a date of the 21st of July that I contest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Usher, please, you need to go and help him find the page on the notebook that he has in front of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It seems to be page 53 of that book.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 56, Your Honour. 00801510.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Here on the e-court it shows page 53.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the right page, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So. All right. Witness, have a look at that page, you will notice that halfway down the page there is an intercept, the beginning -- which at the beginning indicates the date, that being 21st of July of 1995. Now, your question, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: My question is as follows: On the first page, on the cover page, of this notebook, we were able to see a date, the 16th of July, 1995, and before that date, the 21 of July, 1995. So before that date, there were at least ten other days that can be identified, if we look at intercepted conversations. So I'm just wondering how is this possible?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The three of us are not understanding the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: A problem of the translation, maybe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It may well be a problem of translation, but to us the way it has been translated means how is it possible that there is an interval of -- I mean, perhaps you can explain your question better.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection to foundation. If she can establish he knows about who or why or what the first page means or who did it, if he knows anything about that, that question may be able to be answered, but until that's established this is -- again it's a quiz.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But apart from that, Mr. McCloskey, I think we first need to understand what the question was.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question is the following: There are at least ten different days in this notebook that can be identified if we look at this notebook and the date that appears here. On the 21st, it would have been the fifth conversation as of the 16th of July, so it's not very logical for me. So this is why I was asking the witness to explain. If he doesn't know what it means as of the 16th of July, 1995, he of course cannot answer my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Explain what? What do you want him to explain?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How is it possible that between the 16th of July and the 21st of July, 10 days could have gone by?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you understanding the question, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that will become a submission.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President, I cannot do it differently. I cannot testify instead of the witness. In order to show this, we would have to go through the notebook to show that there are days that follow each other and that when it says the 21st of July that's not logical. The date does not appear to be logical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The witness cannot help you. He's told you straight and plain that he doesn't know. He's not even understanding your question, and to be honest, neither am I. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We have to go back to the supervisor that spoke about this, if you recall, the dates that got put on the front page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I won't give you the information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is why I'm saying it should become a submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau, the only logical way we can go about this, if you want to pursue it, is to identify the 10 days that you are maintaining can be gleaned from the preceding pages in this notebook and then put the question again to the witness. But otherwise I simply cannot follow, and I'm not surprised that the witness cannot follow.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. President. This is exactly what I wanted to do because that was the purpose of showing the notebook to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, so let's start with these ten different days.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 00801461, it's on page 4 on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If it would help, I would trust Ms. Fauveau to have added up the days correctly as opposed to going over each of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You see, this is -- I don't think we are going to get far, but this is why I said that this is a matter of a submission rather than putting it to the witness, who is not answerable for everything that is included in or shows up in this notebook in any case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Move on. At least the witness would be able to identify the dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. You've seen the first one. And, Usher, if you show the witness how to move through the pages. Witness, you have to look at the last four digits on the top of the page. You see in this page, it is 1461, the last four digits are 1461, and Madam Fauveau will be moving you through this notebook and asking you questions. Yes, next, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, taking into account that there is a date that's written on the first page of this notebook, do you agree with me that this conversation, which is the first conversation transcribed in this notebook could not have been written down before the 16th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. That's a misstatement of the evidence before this Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think this question needs to be answered. It's also a means available for Defence of controlling previous evidence that we have on the dates which appear on the cover of notebooks. So, Witness, you've seen the date on the cover which if I remember well was the 16th of July of 1995. And it's being put to you that this first transcript that -- intercept that you have on page 4 couldn't have happened before, couldn't have been taken before the date which appears on the first page, on the cover of the notebook. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Your next question, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, on page which ends with numbers 1461, you have there the first intercept in the notebook. There are no dates above this intercept, but I presume that it is on the 16th of July that it was transcribed. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And this intercept took place at 1941 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, could it have been the 17th of July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I truly don't know. I can't help you there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you please take 1463? This intercept took place at 2253, so this is the last conversation that took place on that first day, and for the purposes of this cross-examination, let's call it the conversations that took place on the 16th of July. And then if you take the next page, which is 1464, an intercepted conversation took place at 1148. Now do you agree with me that we are talking about the following day, which is now the 17th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Now, can you please go to page 1468. Or, rather, go to 1466, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So this intercepted conversation was recorded at 14.25. We are still talking about the 17th of July; is that right? And then if you take page 1468, the first intercepted conversation was written down at 1300 hours 18, 13.18. So is it logical to say that this conversation took place the day after, on the 18th of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Logical, yes, looking at this notebook.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: The following conversation took place at 16.22. It's on the same page, and when we go to the next page, the page which ends with 1469, we see that an intercepted conversation was written down at 16.15. So this conversation took place the day after; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Most likely.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So it would be the 19th of July; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So please go to page 1472. We see an intercept that took place at 22.06. This is the last conversation of the 19th of July since, if you go to page 1474, the next conversation took place at 8.57 a.m. So do you agree with me that we are talking about the 20th of July now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And if we go to page 1484, you have an intercept which was jotted down at 23.41, and this is the last conversation of the 20th of July. And then there is another intercept which begins at 6.25 a.m., and that intercept should have been taken on the 21st of July, but in this notebook it says 19th of July. Can you explain this to us? How is it that we see the 19th of July on this page?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-137
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't explain it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So can we conclude for the purposes of this cross-examination that this date should have been the 21st of July? Now if you go to page 1496, you will see that an intercept took place at 23.30, and this is the last intercept of that day, of the 21st of July; is this right? And then on the next page, the following intercept took place at 21.48, and this could be on the 22nd of July. So if you go to the next page, which is 1498, you have a conversation that was taken down at 22.47 and the following conversation takes place at 8.11 a.m.?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. Putting the issue to the witness and more prejudicial than probative. The time consuming factor versus the probative value of this is something --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which is what I tried to convey to Madam Fauveau, that at the end of the day this is not a notebook that has been completed from beginning to end by the witness and even suggesting the dates as if they couldn't be otherwise and as if there is no other explanation is leading us no where. This is why I said in the beginning that this will become a matter, subject matter of an ad hoc submission. But we are going to get no where with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I think the message that you wanted to convey is also very clear that looking on the face of it at this notebook if one were to accept the -- that messages or intercepts were entered in a chronological order, then you would be advancing dates much beyond what sometimes appear on particular intercepts. But, again, I mean, getting a confirmation of this from the witness doesn't help you in the least, or it doesn't help your argument in the least.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I fully agree with you that it was -- it is perhaps not necessary to continue, but I wanted to show nevertheless that it was really important to show that the dates that we see in the notebook do not really fit the previous dates and the following dates. So I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thanks. I take it there are no questions from the remaining two Defence teams. Yes, is there re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which means that we finish here with your testimony, sir. On behalf of the Tribunal, I would like to thank you for having come over to give evidence in this case. Madam Usher will escort you out of the courtroom and the rest of the staff will assist you as needed to facilitate your return back home. On behalf of everyone here, I wish you a safe journey back home. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's go through the documents. You have been handed out a list, I suppose. All right. With the caveat that all intercepts are being admitted as indicated earlier on, are there any objections? I hear none. Madam Registrar, the first two will be under seal. The ones which are highlighted will all be under seal. Matters of translation will be taken care of as agreed this morning. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just to clarify one point. One of the -- number 2 in this tab is an intercept that we did not have a 65 ter number for, and actually I'm putting on Mr. Bourgon's hat. That will be the subject to a motion to get a 65 ter number for it. We have nine such intercepts that we have -- that missed the first cut of 65 ters and that will be the subject matter of a motion. In other words, I have a large list of the intercepts, but I don't need to go through that. It's 1 through 14. Not number 15 in the packet because he didn't identify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Yes, Madam Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just for the sake of clarity, and I assume that the complete notebooks will be the subject of a submission, since originally they were not part of the 65 ter list because all the notebooks with all the intercepts did have a 65 ter number and they were part of the Prosecution submissions before the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think we've gone through that debate. We had the same position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that has already been dealt with. All right. So these documents are admitted as are -- with the caveats that I have explained earlier. The Defence teams, are you tendering any documents? Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So we can leave it at that. We stand adjourned until tomorrow morning when we will proceed with Witness number 76. I thank you so much. Have a nice afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 13th day of December, 2006, at 9.00 a.m. 24 25
